On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is the dominant, forceful actor and Sitaram is the yielding obstacle: sword in hand, Udayaditya confronts the guard at the locked door, and Sitaram—who refuses to take up arms because Udayaditya has saved his life twice—submissively touches the prince's foot-dust to his head and even begs to be disarmed and bound head to foot so he can escape the Maharaj's wrath. Udayaditya takes his weapon, ties him up with his own cloth, and overpowers the other guard as well, acting as the rescuer while Sitaram passively sacrifices himself.

On the night of Udayaditya's own escape, the roles are completely reversed: Sitaram becomes the active, mastermind savior, while Udayaditya is the helpless, passive one. It is Sitaram who orchestrates everything—arranging the palace fire with loyal helpers, sabotaging the firefighting, opening the prison door during the chaos, grabbing Udayaditya and almost carrying him out, leading him to Basanta Ray's boat, and then staging Udayaditya's death by burning the empty cell and throwing in bones, a skull, and the prince's sword. Udayaditya, dazed after long confinement, can only ask helplessly, "What should I do? Where should I go?" Thus the man whom Udayaditya once overpowered and bound now unbinds and carries him to freedom—repaying his life-debt by trading places with him as rescuer and rescued.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to have two Pathan assassins ambush and kill Basanta Ray on the road when he stopped at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. This plan failed because one of the Pathans (Khan Saheb) could not bring himself to commit the deed—he instead confessed the plot to Udayaditya, sought Basanta Ray's protection, and Basanta Ray went on safely to Jessore and even confronted Pratapaditya face to face.

The method that finally succeeded was a formal, written death order signed by Pratapaditya himself. Muktiyar Khan arrived with soldiers (disguised in plain clothes) at Raigarh and delivered the order while Basanta Ray was performing his evening prayers. After reading it, the old king completed his devotions, prostrated himself before his deity, and chanted on his prayer beads; then, at his own signal ("Saheb, now!"), the executioner Abdul entered with a drawn sword and beheaded him, emerging from the room with a bloodied sword.

1. **In the inner quarters of the Jessore palace (the Mahishi's room):** Ramai was disguised as a middle-aged woman, with his head covered by a cloth. When Rammohan recognized and exposed him, he seized Ramai's hands, lifted and swung him through the air, grabbed him by the throat, and finally tied him up with a shawl and slung him over his shoulder like a sack.

2. **In the royal chamber/court at Chandradwip (when Vibha arrived dressed as a humble maidservant):** Ramai appeared undisguised, in his usual role as the jester. After he mocked Vibha by asking if her "dada" was no longer to her liking, Rammohan forcefully grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and threw him out of the room.

Mangala (Rukmini) secretly poisoned her. When the Mahishi heard of a widow named Mangala skilled in tantra, mantra, and medicine, she sent Matangini to obtain a remedy meant to win Udayaditya's heart back from Surma before sending her away. Mangala spent five days preparing what was presented as medicine but was actually poison, chanting mantras so that Udayaditya would feel no pity when Surma died. On the eve of her departure, after consuming it, Surma fell gravely ill and died—though the palace believed she had taken her own life by poison.

Because Vibha refused to go with Rammohan Mal on his first visit, King Ramchandra Ray took another wife. By the time Vibha finally set out for Chandradwip, "in your own kingdom there is no place for you—in your own royal palace, there is no home for you." When she arrived at the palace dressed as a common woman, the king rejected and disowned her ("Who is my Mahishi? I do not know her!"), humiliating her before the court, after which she departed with Udayaditya to spend her life in Kashi.

During a stormy night, Rukmini deceives the grieving Udayaditya—playing on his guilt and loneliness—and tricks him into giving her the signet ring from his finger before leaving. She then conspires with Sitaram and Bhagavat (the two are seen plotting together in secret). Shortly afterward, Bhagavat presents Pratapaditya with a forged petition—apparently authenticated by means of the prince's ring—as evidence that Udayaditya has committed an offense. Although the minister protests that such a thing is impossible to believe of the Yubaraj, Pratapaditya flies into a rage and, after consideration, orders Udayaditya imprisoned—insisting he does not fully believe the charge either, but sees no harm in confining him under guard.

Ramchandra Ray's midnight escape could only succeed because Prince Udayaditya overpowered and bound the palace guards (Sitaram and Bhagavat) and opened the locked inner quarters. To shield Udayaditya from Pratapaditya's wrath, Basanta Ray instructed the guards to claim that he himself had tied them up; when the guard Bhagavat refused to lie, Basanta Ray secretly paid him money to secure his silence. When word of these secret stipends (the bribes) reached Pratapaditya's ears, he responded by issuing an order that Surma must go to her paternal home, ostensibly for the sake of "state affairs" — i.e., to remove her far from the royal palace. When Surma protested that she had no reason to go, Pratapaditya threatened to imprison Udayaditya if she did not obey, thereby forcing her to accept the exile. Thus, the cover-up of the escape — the hush-money given to the guards — became known to the king and indirectly triggered his decree banishing Surma.

The song "I alone am left behind" expresses Basanta Ray's profound loneliness and desolation in old age—the anguish of a man whose loved ones have all been taken from him. Its words capture the sense that everything that was once his has vanished, leaving only emptiness; those who were once his no longer answer his call, and without them he feels he has no spirit left to go on living. It rises spontaneously from his heart because the people he used to sing for—Udayaditya and Surma—are no longer there, so the song comes on its own but brings no joy.

He sings it in two contrasting contexts:

1. **Alone at sunset in Raigarh:** Sitting on his palace veranda without his sitar (which he had left behind in Jessore), he hums it to himself as a private, wistful lament of separation—longing for the loved ones far away in Jessore, remembering how joy would once send him rushing to them. When Khan Saheb arrives and asks to hear his song, he repeats it in this same setting, somberly noting that though the sitar exists, its strings have broken and can no longer be tuned—a metaphor for his own state.

2. **In Jessore, before the empty room:** After learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, he goes to Vibha and stands before Surma's room—now silent, dark, and utterly empty, though it once erupted with joy at his visits. Taking Vibha's hand, he slowly sings "I alone am left behind!" as a heart-rending cry, with the loss no longer a distant ache but a concrete, present reality witnessed amid the desolation of the broken household.

Rukmini's failure set off the chain of events that ended in Basanta Ray's execution:

1. **The failed interception:** When Udayaditya escaped by boat after the prison fire, Rukmini rushed to the bank, pounced on Sitaram, and tried to reach Udayaditya, but was forcibly pulled away by the boatmen. Enraged and despairing, she cursed them and threw herself into the canal — but the escape succeeded anyway.

2. **The fake death:** Because the escape went through, Sitaram was able to stage his cover-up — setting fire to Udayaditya's empty cell, throwing in bones, a skull, and the prince's sword, and spreading the rumor that the Yubaraj had burned to death. Pratapaditya believed his son was dead, and Basanta Ray was found missing from the palace.

3. **Rukmini's vengeful revelation:** Having survived her suicide attempt and consumed by fury at her repeatedly thwarted revenge, Rukmini forced her way into Pratapaditya's assembly hall. There she exposed the whole plot: the Yubaraj was not dead but had escaped the previous night with "the old king" (Basanta Ray), and it was Sitaram who had set the fire. She revealed that all three — the Yubaraj, Sitaram, and Basanta Ray — had conspired together.

4. **The king's response:** On the strength of her information, Pratapaditya sent men with Rukmini, received confirmation that Udayaditya was in Raigarh, and then summoned the Pathan commander Muktiyar Khan with a secret order.

5. **The execution:** That secret order contained the death sentence for the King of Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan captured Udayaditya (with Rukmini pointing him out) and proceeded to Raigarh, where he presented Pratapaditya's signed order to Basanta Ray, who was beheaded by Abdul.

Thus, because Rukmini could not stop the midnight escape, her thwarted rage drove her to betray the conspiracy to Pratapaditya — exposing Basanta Ray as Udayaditya's abettor and prompting the royal death order that Muktiyar Khan carried out.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra Ray with cold, understated condescension: when Ramchandra arrives at Jessore determined to display his own greatness, Pratapaditya shows no joy or haste, greets him with a flat "Come. Are you well?", interrupts him to attend to routine ministerial business, and curtly dismisses him with "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters." Without any open hostility, this treatment makes Ramchandra realize "in what way Pratapaditya was superior to him."

Back in his own court at Chandradwip, Ramchandra responds not with equal dignity but with petty retaliation against Pratapaditya's status. He has a subject tried and terrorized merely for discussing or comparing the two kings, while his minister and Dewan publicly degrade Pratapaditya's lineage—claiming Pratapaditya's father had to weep and plead for royal anointment from Ramchandra's grandfather, who anointed him with the little toe of his left foot—and Ramai Bhand ridicules Pratapaditya's ancestry as descended from "earthworms" and "leeches." The king, immensely pleased, encourages these daily verbal attacks on Pratapaditya, laughing along as the courtiers mock both Pratapaditya and Udayaditya.

In short, Pratapaditya asserted his superiority through calm indifference and effortless command, which genuinely humbled Ramchandra; Ramchandra, unable to match that authority, compensates in his own court by fostering sycophantic mockery and fabricated claims of ancestral inferiority, exposing his own small-mindedness rather than restoring his honor.

The older widow is Rukmini. Having left Raigarh and changed her name to Mangala, she settled on the outskirts of Jessore, where she nurtured the hope of ruling over Udayaditya's heart once he became king. She re-entered his life through several acts of treachery:

1. **Killing Surma**: She befriended the palace servants and tracked palace news. When the Rajmahishi heard that a widow named Mangala knew tantra, mantra, and medicine, she sent Matangini to fetch medicine from her. Mangala spent five days preparing poison with mantras and rituals, and Surma died after taking it.

2. **Obtaining his royal seal**: During a stormy night, she visited the grieving Udayaditya, wept that he had ruined her, and demanded his love; when he refused, she took the ring from his finger, which bore the Yubaraj's seal. This seal was used to forge a petition of treason against Pratapaditya in Udayaditya's name, leading to Udayaditya's imprisonment.

3. **Betraying his escape**: When Udayaditya escaped and was being smuggled away by boat, she tried to attack him, bit Sitaram, cursed him, and drowned herself in the canal.

4. **Causing Basanta Ray's death**: She tracked Udayaditya to Raigarh and pointed out his hiding place to the soldiers, crying "Here is your Yubaraj!" This led to Udayaditya's capture and to Pratapaditya's order being carried out—the execution of Basanta Ray.

Udayaditya's early lament—that he wished he had never been born in a royal palace, that he had been "a subject of the lowliest" rather than the crown prince and sole heir, and that he wondered "what penance could I perform to reverse this past"—stems from his feeling that in a king's family one is born only as an heir, not as a son, and that his father regards him as unfit, a "disgrace to the family." This wish to shed his royal identity is repeatedly intensified: his father's contempt and neglect, the expulsion of Surma from the palace, her death by poison, his unjust imprisonment on a forged petition, and his dramatic escape during the prison fire all deepen his sense that his position as heir brings only suffering to himself and ruin to those he loves.

The culmination comes when, after fleeing to Raigarh with Basanta Ray, he chooses to return to Jessore to face his father, fearing the consequences Basanta Ray might suffer for sheltering him. On the journey back, his old lament reaches its final form: he cries that nothing has been accomplished by his birth, that "utter ruin has been caused because of me," that the weak only burden and destroy those who cling to them, and he declares, "No more, I am taking my leave of this world."

Brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he formally converts this lifelong lament into renunciation. When his father pronounces him "not worthy of this kingdom," Udayaditya agrees—"I am not worthy. I do not want your kingdom—grant me release from your throne—this is my plea." To prove his sincerity, he takes a solemn oath before Ma-Kali in the temple, in Pratapaditya's presence, swearing never to accept even an iota of the Maharaja of Jessore's kingdom, never to sit on its throne, nor touch its royal scepter, invoking the sin of his grand-uncle's murder upon himself if he ever breaks the vow. He names Samaraditya as heir, asks only to be freed—not caged like a beast—and departs for Kashi to live as an ascetic, planning to establish a guest house and temple in Basanta Ray's name. Thus the boy who once wished, in despair, that he had never been born a prince finally achieves that wish through an oath-bound, formal renunciation of the throne itself.

Nayanchand, the old messenger entrusted with delivering the letter, was too afraid of what Pratapaditya might do if he received such a letter, so instead of delivering it to him, he secretly handed it over to the Mahishi. The Mahishi kept its contents hidden from both Pratapaditya and the delicate Vibha, fearing the news would destroy her, and confided only in Basanta Ray. On his advice—since he believed Ramchandra had written merely out of anger that would subside once Vibha returned—the household was told that Ramchandra had written a letter *requesting* that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip. Thus the letter, which actually declared that Ramchandra had renounced Vibha and demanded she never be sent to Chandradwip again, was misrepresented to her as an invitation summoning her to her husband's home.

Pratapaditya tried to trap Ramchandra Ray by ordering the canal adjoining the royal palace—where Ramchandra's sixty-four-oared boat lay—to be blocked immediately with large logs of Sal wood, while also forbidding anyone to leave the inner quarters. The trap failed for several reasons during the midnight escape:

1. **The escape bypassed the locked exits entirely**: After Udayaditya overpowered the guards and opened the way out of the inner quarters, Rammohan lowered Ramchandra Ray from the palace roof directly into the canal using a rope made of thick tied sheets, so the boat reached the water despite all doors being locked.

2. **The guards could not stop the boat at the log barrier**: When the boat was halted by the sal wood logs, the guards threw stones, but not a single one reached it. They had swords but no guns; one guard went to fetch a gun, and while they frantically searched shouting for gunpowder and bullets, Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs.

3. **The pursuit boat arrived too late**: The man sent to fetch a chase boat stopped on the way at Harimudi's shop to smoke a pipeful of tobacco and went to wake Ramashankar from his bed to press him for payment of a debt. By the time the boat finally arrived amid much shouting and scolding, there was no longer any chance of catching Ramchandra's boat, which escaped to the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray's sitar serves as a barometer of his inner state, tracing his descent from joy to despair. At first, the sitar is his cherished "eternal companion," having replaced the sword in his hand; he plays it exuberantly—standing up, forgetting dignity—and declares that his two "foolish youngsters," Udayaditya and Vibha, are his only audience, and that without them he would have shut down his "singing shop" long ago. When he is finally reunited with them, his music flows freely to "unburden his soul."

As misfortune closes in, the relationship deteriorates. During the painful farewell in Jessore, he snatches up the sitar and plays it furiously, but Vibha's tears blur his eyes, choke his throat, and force him to stop; he leaves the sitar behind with the words, "I will not play it anymore"—abandoning the very source of his joy because those he played for are being torn from him.

Later, alone in Raigarh, the sitar is "no longer with him," and he can only hum mournful songs—"I alone am left behind... what remains is only emptiness"—admitting that although the song rises on its own, there is no longer any joy in singing it. When Khan Saheb asks where the sitar is, Basanta Ray reveals the fullest image of his despair: "The sitar is there, only its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned." The broken, untunable strings mirror his own broken heart—a music-maker whose music has died along with his hope of seeing Udayaditya, culminating in his desperate, tearful pleas to Pratapaditya and his anguished cry, "Dada, come to me! No one understood you."

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for openly championing the oppressed: as a young administrator at Hosenkhali he won the subjects' blessings (at the cost of his father's approval), and he routinely mixed with common people and took their side against Pratapaditya, intervening without considering the consequences—so routinely that these acts had become minor, expected news. After Surma's death, this willingness collapses. A strange, blind fear of Pratapaditya takes hold of him, his former courage disappears, and he can no longer fight oppression. When he learns that club-wielding men are to loot and burn the zamindar of Chhapra's estate office, he readies his horse but then absentmindedly tells the servant to take it away. When he sees an official beating a crying subject tied to a tree who begs him for mercy, he cannot bear the sight and instead runs into his house—whereas before he would have stopped the official without a thought. Likewise, he no longer has the courage to help the dismissed guards Sitaram and Bhagavat, openly or secretly; though he resolves to send them money, he hesitates each time and never sends it.

The damage Sitaram caused with Bhagavat was the forged treason petition—stamped with Udayaditya's seal and delivered to Pratapaditya—which resulted in the Yubaraj's imprisonment. Sitaram ultimately undoes this by orchestrating Udayaditya's escape from prison: he stages a fire in the palace (with the help of loyal commoners and servants, some of whom sabotage the firefighting), throws open Udayaditya's cell and carries him out to safety during the chaos, then sets fire to the now-empty cell, throwing in bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword to fake the prince's death in the blaze. By spreading the rumor that the Yubaraj burned to death, Sitaram enables Udayaditya to escape freely by boat, thereby reversing the imprisonment his own conspiracy had brought about.

On the first occasion, after the doors of Pratapaditya's palace were locked, Rammohan carried King Ramchandra Ray on his back from the palace roof: he twisted several thick bed sheets into a makeshift rope, tied it to a small roof pillar, and climbed down it toward the canal about seventy cubits below; at the rope's end he held it with his teeth, lowered the king with both hands into the sixty-four-oared boat, and then jumped down himself.

On the second occasion, when the king of Chandradwip insulted and disowned the fainted Vibha, Rammohan lifted her in his arms, carried her out of the hostile palace, and placed the unconscious, exhausted princess into a palanquin near the gate before returning to the boat.

In Jessore, when preparing to receive her husband, Vibha is lavishly adorned as a royal bride by her mother, the Mahishi: against her own simpler taste (she would have preferred just three thin turquoise bangles per hand), she is made to wear eight thick gold bangles and one huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring on her delicate face, and an elaborate hairstyle styled by the Mahishi herself—leaving her weighed down with jewels, coiffure, and barely contained joy.

By contrast, when she finally goes to seek out Ramchandra Ray in Chandradwip after learning of his remarriage, she strips away all royal presentation: refusing a palanquin ("Am I a queen that I should ask for a palanquin?"), she insists on going "like a common subject, like a beggar-woman." Dressed as an ordinary common woman, she walks on foot through crowds, keeps her head covered with a veil (which slips and must hastily be restored), and enters the palace unnoticed—"like any other maidservant," with no welcome—so completely transformed that even the king fails to recognize her and takes her for a beggar woman come seeking alms.

In the bedchamber after Surma's death, the window symbolizes Surma herself—shared intimacy, memory, and loss. It was the spot where she and Udayaditya used to sit together every evening, and after her death he returns to it again and again, leaving her place empty, hoping against hope that he will find her sitting there when he opens the door. The same moonlight, garden, and breeze only deepen his grief, making the window a site of mourning and painful absence.

In the prison cell, by contrast, the small window comes to symbolize freedom and hope of liberation. Through its narrow opening Udayaditya can see a sliver of sky, a bamboo grove, and a Shiva temple, and watching the birds fly, he imagines that his own cage will one day break and he will soar into the endless sky. He tells Vibha that this two-hands'-breadth patch by the window is the one place where he feels naturally free—"no king or emperor can hold me captive"—while the soft bed away from the window feels like the true prison.

Thus the window shifts from being an emblem of bereavement and the irretrievable past with Surma to an emblem of hope, inner freedom, and the promise of future release.

Sitaram and Rukmini's relationship begins as a mutually useful, flirtatious arrangement: the penniless but stylish guard, drawn to the wealthy widow's beauty and money, visits her home to borrow cash under false pretenses, and she lends it while feigning affection. Their exchanges are playful—Sitaram performs witty banter ("You are my Subhadra, and I am your Jagannath"), and Rukmini teases him into calling her "Pran," "Priye," "Priyatame," and "Pranpriye" before coyly raising the question of interest, which he laughs off as a joke. The relationship then turns secretive and scheming, as the two confer together on a plot that requires Bhagavat's help, even as Rukmini secretly pursues her own obsession with winning the Yubaraj Udayaditya.

The bond collapses when Udayaditya is imprisoned: Sitaram storms into Rukmini's house, curses her, all but strikes her, and vows to burn her house down, free the Yubaraj, and smear her face with lime and soot. Rukmini suppresses her explosive rage and coldly asserts that the Yubaraj is *hers*, warning Sitaram not to interfere. Open violence follows during Udayaditya's escape: Rukmini, wild with thwarted revenge, pounces on Sitaram when he shields the prince, sinking her grip into him until he cries out and bleeds from the shoulder; after being torn away, she claws her own chest, curses him with the sin of killing a woman, and hurls herself into the flooded canal.

The final, most direct threat to Sitaram's life comes when, believing Rukmini drowned and dead, he sneaks into her dark cottage to steal her money—and finds her alive, dripping wet and spectral. His attempt to revive their old intimacy with feigned affection ("Are you sulking, my dear? Shall I sing that song?") only inflames her fury. Declaring she will cremate him and the Yubaraj before dying herself, she searches for a curved blade to kill him; realizing his metaphorical talk of dying has become literal danger, Sitaram slips out just in time, leaving Rukmini hacking the floor where he had stood. That same night, fearing she will expose the escape plot, he flees Jessore with his family—while Rukmini goes to Pratapaditya's court to denounce Sitaram as the arsonist behind the Yubaraj's staged death.

Sitaram's plan began as a mere diversion: he arranged for fires to break out simultaneously in five or six rooms of the guards' huts near the prison, using loyal commoners and palace servants. The blaze drew every available guard away from duty—those posted at Udayaditya's door were the first to flee—leaving the prison unguarded so Sitaram could walk in and carry the Yubaraj out to freedom.

It then deepened into deliberate sabotage: Sitaram planted his own men among the firefighters, who poured water where there was no fire, fetched water without returning, broke their pots, and stumbled into one another, ensuring the fire raged on and the chaos persisted.

Next, the distraction became a cover-up of the escape itself. While everyone was absorbed in fighting the guardhouse fire, Sitaram's men secretly set Udayaditya's now-empty prison cell ablaze—burning the windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, and fences until the structure collapsed. To fabricate the prince's death, Sitaram threw bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the burning room. Staged cries that the Yubaraj was heard screaming inside, followed by the announcement that the roof had collapsed with no response from him, produced "witnesses" who later testified before Pratapaditya that they had seen Udayaditya through the window, heard his screams, and recovered the melted remains of his sword.

Finally, Sitaram sealed the deception by controlling information: although Udayaditya had written three letters to the palace, Sitaram secretly forbade the messenger from delivering them, retrieved them upon returning, kept only those addressed to the Mahishi and Vibha, and destroyed the rest. His aim, as he himself reflected, was to spread the news that the Yubaraj had perished in the fire and thus remain undisturbed—at least until Rukmini exposed the truth to the king.

In his court, Ramchandra Ray shows no gratitude toward Udayaditya at all. Instead, he joins his courtiers in laughing at and ridiculing Udayaditya simply because he is Pratapaditya's son. He dismisses the life-saving act as something that was "bound to happen"—something anyone would be obliged to do for him—and rationalizes that Udayaditya saved him only for the sake of his own sister Vibha, not out of any real concern for Ramchandra himself. Lacking the mental strength to silence the mockers like Ramai Bhand, he even participates in the jokes, fearing what everyone would think if he defended his brother-in-law.

Pratapaditya repeatedly scoffed at the Emperor of Delhi as a source of fear: when his minister warned that the Emperor would be angered by Basanta Ray's murder, Pratapaditya declared that "the Emperor of Delhi is not my God," refused to be dissuaded by the threat of the Emperor's "fifty thousand soldiers," found such warnings deeply insulting, and even forbade the minister from uttering the Emperor's name until the assassination was complete. Likewise, when told that a complaint had been lodged against him with the Emperor, he brushed it aside, boasting, "I am the judge of the Emperor of Delhi; I myself am arranging his punishment."

Yet this same despised imperial authority ultimately becomes the trap that ensnares his son. After being dismissed and punished for their negligence, the two guards Sitaram and Bhagavat conspire to regain their positions. They forge a petition, stamped with Udayaditya's own seal (taken from a ring Rukmini had brought), making it appear that the Yubaraj himself was lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi in order to seize the kingdom for himself. Knowing the foolish Sitaram could not be trusted with the task, Bhagavat carries the forged document not to Delhi but directly to Pratapaditya, presenting it as evidence he intercepted—a servant of Udayaditya supposedly caught fleeing toward Delhi with it. Reading the petition, Pratapaditya is thrown into a terrible state (resulting in Udayaditya's imprisonment), and Bhagavat is rewarded with the restoration of his palace job. Thus, the imperial power Pratapaditya once mocked as an empty threat becomes the very instrument through which his son is accused of treachery and cast into prison.

The grooming of Vibha's hair marks Surma's presence through an act of tender intimacy: in Chapter 6, when Vibha is overwhelmed with grief over her husband's disrespect and hides her face in Surma's lap, Surma comforts her by gently running her fingers through Vibha's thick hair as they sit together in silence, wiping her tears. After Surma's tragic death by poison, this same act of hair-care becomes a painful emblem of her absence: in Chapter 18, Vibha sits quietly when it is time to braid her hair, waiting as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it for her, but evening falls, night approaches, and Surma never comes—leaving Vibha's hair unbraided. The unbraided hair thus transforms from a symbol of Surma's soothing, nurturing presence into a silent testament to the void she has left behind in the palace, underscoring Vibha's desolation and her inability to accept that Surma is truly gone.
